what_its_for: Isatuximab-irfc is a cancer medicine used to treat multiple myeloma, which is a type of blood cancer that affects plasma cells in your bone marrow. It is usually given together with other cancer medicines. It works by attaching to cancer cells and helping your immune system find and destroy them.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is slowly dripped into your vein through a needle or catheter. A nurse or healthcare provider will give you this infusion in a clinic or hospital setting. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Before each infusion, you will be given pre-medications (such as antihistamines, steroids, and fever reducers) to help prevent infusion reactions. Each infusion can take several hours, so plan your day accordingly. Stay at the clinic until your healthcare team says it is safe for you to leave.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your body weight and treatment plan. The typical dosing schedule starts with weekly infusions for the first two months, and then switches to every-two-week infusions after that. Always follow your doctor's specific schedule. Do not skip or delay infusions without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given in a clinic by a healthcare professional, contact your doctor or care team as soon as possible if you miss or need to reschedule an infusion. Do not try to catch up on your own. Your doctor will reschedule your infusion and may adjust your treatment calendar if needed.
storage: This medicine is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals at the clinic or hospital. You do not need to store it at home. If you are given any take-home medicines as part of your treatment plan, follow the storage instructions on those separate labels.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting treatment, as some may interact with isatuximab-irfc. Avoid live vaccines while on treatment unless your doctor approves them. This medicine can interfere with certain blood typing tests called indirect antiglobulin tests (also called a Coombs test), so always remind any doctor, dentist, or blood bank staff that you are taking this medicine. Try to avoid people who are sick or have infections, as this medicine can lower your ability to fight infections.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: difficulty breathing, chest pain, or tightness during or after your infusion; severe chills, fever, or shaking; low blood pressure, dizziness, or fainting; signs of infection such as fever over 100.4°F, cough, or painful urination; unusual bleeding or bruising; extreme tiredness or weakness; or any new or worsening symptoms. Infusion reactions are most common during the first infusion, so let your nurse know immediately if you feel unwell during treatment.
when_it_works: Cancer medicines like isatuximab-irfc may take several weeks or months before you notice results. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular blood tests and exams. Keep all of your scheduled appointments and infusions, even if you feel well, because missing treatment can affect how well the medicine works.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medicine can harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 5 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while receiving this medicine. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Elderly patients: Older adults can be treated with this medicine, but your doctor will monitor you closely for side effects. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor will review your kidney and liver function before and during treatment. Always tell your healthcare team about all your medical conditions.
